title: ‘I found my place at EF’: Noemi Rüegg Q&A
content:
Cyclist
‘I found my place at EF’: Noemi Rüegg Q&A

How are you feeling about the upcoming World Championships?

I’m feeling good. Really excited. I’ve been looking forward to it for a long time, and I think we have a really strong Swiss team, so we have many cards to play. It’s gonna be an exciting race I think.

You’ve had the World Champion, Magdeleine Vallieres, on your team this past season. That must be quite inspiring. Does it make you dream about what’s possible?

Yeah, totally. I think last year’s Worlds showed that it’s a super-open race, and basically anyone can win. It’s very tactical, so you have to play it really smart because it’s a different race than any we do with our normal team. We have no radio, so it’s really hard to keep it under control. Last year showed that anything can happen. And it was so nice to see Mags winning. She deserved it so much, and seeing how she developed through the last year and how this jersey gave her wings was really inspiring.

You’ve had quite a tough year with a crash at La Vuelta. Is that the toughest thing you’ve had to come back from?

Yeah I think this injury was the biggest challenge I’ve had in my career yet. I broke my collarbone the year before, but my broken arm was definitely worse, and it took me quite a while to come back. But I’m really happy that I could come back strong.

In the moment it was really hard, and I doubted myself a lot – I couldn’t really find the answer why this had to happen. But I think in the end, these three months also taught me a lot, and I think I got out of it not physically stronger, but mentally a lot stronger. It’s a new experience that I have with me now, and I think it will help me in the upcoming years.

How did you get through those difficult months?

I was super-lucky. I could count on a very strong environment. My family were behind me since day one. My mum flew to the hospital in Spain, and then she came back with me to Switzerland. She was a really big help this whole time. But also, the whole staff of the team, the team doctors organised everything really well together with our doctors in Switzerland. The whole medical staff of Swiss Olympic worked super hard, and my national coach as well. So it was like one big family, everyone together, trying to help me get back on my bike as quick as possible, and I felt really supported.

So I never felt really alone in this situation. I always knew I had a whole group behind me that wants the best for me and really cares about me, and that gave me a calm mindset that it’s gonna be fine; the injury happened, and now it’s out of my control, and I can only control how I react to it. I wanted to do that with 100% commitment, just to use every day the best that I could to get back as quick as possible, depending on the day, doing what my body could do the best possible way. The time actually went really quick. I went to the physio a lot and tried to do some other things as well besides cycling. Just spend time with family and friends, and I think that helped the recovery process as well.

What else did you do to pass the time?

I was stressed or quite busy all the time. I was never really bored because in the first few days obviously everything takes more time, even to get dressed or to shower. So you’re busy with those things, and then I had to go to the physio every second day. I had appointments with the doctors. So time was actually passing really quick. I could already go back on the trainer one week after the surgery. In the beginning was only really short training, but then I had something to do. So actually I wasn’t really bored. I went to some ice hockey games, which I really enjoyed. Did a lot of baking and cooking in the kitchen, things like that.

Talk us through your journey into cycling.

I have an older brother, Timon. He’s five years older, and he’s a professional mountain biker. And my father used to be a cyclist as well when he was younger. So cycling was always a family thing. My brother started racing earlier than me, obviously, and we always went to watch his cyclocross races on the weekend as a family. At first I was really not interested, but then I had to change my school from primary to secondary, and I had to go by bike, and since that moment I totally fell in love with it – I felt the freedom and was like, “Yeah, I want to try this out as well.” I borrowed a bike from a friend and then I rode my first cyclocross race a few weeks after that. Then it became a family thing, every weekend was filled with cyclocross races and then a few years after, I started to race more on the road, and then made the switch.

We often think of Swiss riders as excellent time-triallists, but you have come to the sport from the off-road route. Did growing up in Switzerland influence your direction?

I did some mountain biking as well, [which] is also really big in Switzerland. But I soon realised that wasn’t for me, and actually by the time that I started on the road, we had Fabian Cancellara, but Marlen [Reusser] didn’t race at that time yet, so it was kind of difficult because there were no women I could look up to that were in the WorldTour – I had to find a bit my own way. I think now we actually built up a really strong women’s squad on the road, so that young girls can come after us and have something to look up to and a pathway that is already there for them. But at the time I started, it was a bit challenging to find my own way.

Who inspired you when you were getting into cycling?

Good question. I think by the time I started, it was for sure more male athletes, like Fabian Cancellara was big idol for me, but also because I did a lot of cyclocross, I was always a big fan of Wout van Aert. I still am now. Those were my idols, but also my brother. I always looked up to him, and he helped me a lot in this whole path because everything I had to go through, I knew he went through already, so I could always ask him for help or for his advice. And I always wanted to be as strong as him – that was one of my big motivations as well.

We know you as a really versatile rider. What’s your favourite kind of race to ride?

I really like it if it’s on from the beginning and a hard race with not a lot of rest. I like the punchy climbs, between two- and five-minute efforts, again and again, and then a reduced sprint at the end. For me, one of my favourite races for sure is Milan-San Remo. It’s a big goal for me to win this race one day. But also races like Flanders, where you have all these short but steep climbs, and it’s just a brutal race, or even a race like Liège. So yeah, I’m quite versatile, and I can make use of my really good power-to-weight ratio. I can get over the climbs, but I can also sprint at the end, and I think that’s my superpower.

What’s been your favourite memory in cycling so far?

Probably what I will always remember is the first edition of San Remo, where I finished on the podium in third place. That was just a really amazing experience because it was a big goal, but it was the first edition, so nobody knew how it would play out, and we didn’t know really what to expect. But we had such a great team plan, and everyone committed so well. And then that I was able to finish it off was really amazing. That was my first podium in a Monument.

Also my first WorldTour win in Australia when I won on Willunga Hill in the Tour Down Under, because this was a solo victory, and I think that’s one of the most beautiful wins you can have in cycling if you win solo. I think this was the start of my breakthrough that really gave me the confidence to know I can be up there and I belong with the best of the world, and ever since I was quite consistent in all of the races, actually. So, I would say one of those two.

You’ve won the Tour Down Under twice in a row now, what is it about Australia that works for you so well?

I really like Australia. I just love the atmosphere there. It’s so relaxed, and the people are super-nice. It almost feels a bit like a holiday to get there. But also I can really lock in and have a good training block at home, and I really love training at home. So the winter time is always this period where I’m home most, and I can really focus on training, but also I think I have a really good balance between training and mental recovery. In the winter I do a lot of other stuff. I can go out with friends, go to hockey games and stuff. I think that I always come out so strong because I can focus on training, but I also really enjoy life. And then I go to the race and I feel mentally totally recovered, but physically I’m in really good shape.

Also now after my injury, I had this block at home where I could train and do other things, and I came really strong out of it. So I think there is something for me, about the fact of spending time at home, because we travel so much during the year, sometimes you lose yourself a bit when you travel from one to the other race and training camp, and it just gets too much. And I think then you can’t produce the same performance in the race.

You’ve been at EF for a while now. Tell us what’s working for you there and why it’s such a good team to be a part of.

Yeah, I’m super-happy. I found my place at EF. I think it’s a super-good match for me. Comparing it to other teams, I would say it’s like the fans’ favourite team, I think we really show that cycling is not all about results, but also about having fun and inspiring others, having a great team culture. Everyone gets accepted as the rider they are and the personality behind, and you don’t feel like you need to fit into a certain box.

Of course, we want to have good results, but I think this is the first step. If you have fun and you feel good and happy in your place, and you enjoy the atmosphere, you have the right people around, then the results and the performance will come automatically. I think sometimes teams try to focus too much on results, and it gets so serious that you forget to actually enjoy and have fun, and then you won’t get great results either.

Women’s cycling is developing fast. What further improvements would you like to see to the women’s side of the sport?

Yeah, we’ve come a really long way, and over the past few years it developed super-quick. We probably can’t continue at that speed because I think teams need time to adjust to it. I think at the moment we are in a really good place, and it’s okay to realise, this is actually a good place, and we don’t always need to get more and more and better because I think we will never be really equal to the men. I think it’s not possible, and also it’s not needed.

It’s just about continuing like this and holding this standard, and of course it would be nice to get more sponsors into women’s cycling or get longer TV coverage, but in my opinion, we are already in a really good spot. Comparing it to other women’s sports, I think cycling is one of the most developed.

Finally, what brings you joy off the bike?

Ice hockey games. Just spending a lot of time with family and friends, cooking, baking. I enjoy really good coffee. Just being out in the nature, connecting to myself.
